name: glinski hexagonal chess
description: Władysław Gliński's hexagonal chess: chess rebuilt for a board of 91 hexagonal cells, six to a side. A rook runs along the six lines through a cell's edges, a bishop along the six diagonals between them, which keep it on a third of the board (hence three bishops a side), a queen does both, a king steps in any of those twelve directions and a knight jumps to the twelve nearest cells no line reaches. Twelve ways out of every cell make a king hard to box in, so a mating net takes more pieces to close than on a square board. A pawn promotes on reaching the far edge, the eleven cells where it has no step forward left. Three things depart from Gliński's own rules: there is no en passant, the second army is the first turned half a turn rather than mirrored, so each king faces the other queen, and stalemate is a plain draw where Gliński gave the stalemating side three quarters of a point.

provenance.source: docs/game-ideas.md, Q281 specified: a native hexagon
provenance.history: Schema 16's showcase for board.shape (Q281a4): hex-glinski-promoting with board.shape "hexagon" and its rules.obstacles removed, and nothing else. It compiles to the parent's tables array by array, so it demonstrates by identity, as board.lattice did in schema 14: its measured score is predicted to equal the parent's to the last printed digit under the same basis.
